strengths: Proposes a unified and conceptually appealing framework that connects local search via annealed Langevin MCMC with global tree search (BFS/DFS) for inference-time scaling of diffusion models.

Provides a theoretical unification showing that training-free guidance with recurrence corresponds, in a continuous limit, to Langevin MCMC on annealed distributions, giving insight into why recurrence can reduce OOD/adversarial samples.

Evaluates the framework across multiple domains, including long-horizon maze planning, D4RL offline RL, CompBench text-to-image generation, and ImageNet conditional generation, which demonstrates breadth.
Local search with verifier gradients shows clear benefits in the maze planning task, where naive sampling fails and multiple Langevin MCMC steps substantially improve success rates.

Global BFS-Resampling/BFS-Pruning and DFS-style backtracking can improve compute efficiency over Best-of-N in several image and planning experiments, and DFS shows difficulty-adaptive compute allocation.
The double-verifier heuristic for ImageNet conditional generation is a practical idea that improves both FID and accuracy under Best-of-N sampling.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the work largely combines existing ingredients—annealed Langevin MCMC/compositional generation, training-free guidance, BFS/DFS, and best-first search—and prior work such as Ma et al. [48] already explored search-based inference-time scaling for diffusion models.

The empirical comparisons are incomplete. The paper mainly compares against Best-of-N and does not systematically compare to important prior inference-time scaling/search methods for diffusion, such as Ma et al. [48], SMC/Feynman-Kac steering [62], or other particle/search baselines.

The local-search framework requires differentiable verifiers, which excludes many important non-differentiable verifiers; thus the claimed generality of the local+global framework is overstated. Global search remains largely heuristic with several threshold, temperature, and backtracking hyperparameters and no strong guarantees.

Offline RL results are marginal and often within noise: average 86.1 versus QGPO 86.6 and D-QL 86.3, with some tasks notably worse (e.g., Medium-Replay Walker2d 79.3±9.7 versus D-QL 94.3). The training-free/compute-efficiency claim is not convincingly established there.

ImageNet conditional generation results are weak in absolute terms: FID remains high (e.g., 127.8 for double-verifier Best-of-N) and accuracy stays below 50%, far from competitive class-conditional diffusion baselines. Only two class labels are evaluated.

The CompBench evaluation only tests DFS, not BFS or local+global search, and the evidence is mostly presented in figures without detailed quantitative tables. This makes the efficiency claims less robust.

The planning evaluation relies on a hand-designed oracle verifier derived from ground-truth maze geometry. Comparisons to classical planners or stronger guidance/search baselines would be needed to establish the significance of the reported >90% success rates.

Reproducibility is incompletely supported: the manuscript has a placeholder project page, no code link, some hyperparameters and schedules are only partially specified, and there are notation/typographical issues (e.g., temperature indexing in the BFS formula and phrasing such as “as a instance”).

strengths: Provides a unified conceptual view of inference-time diffusion control by connecting local Langevin-style updates and global BFS/DFS search.
The proposed framework is evaluated across planning, offline RL, and image generation, showing positive empirical trends in several settings.
The paper includes substantial appendix material with implementation details, pseudo-code, and hyperparameter tables.
In offline RL, the method achieves competitive performance with strong training-based baselines while avoiding retraining of the diffusion policy and Q-function.
The compute-efficiency comparisons against Best-of-N in image tasks suggest that adaptive search can reduce verifier calls for equivalent or better performance.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. The local search is largely an instantiation of existing training-free guidance/recurrent guidance methods, and the BFS/DFS global search strategies closely follow prior search-based diffusion inference-scaling work such as Ma et al. and SMC-style steering. The claimed unification is mostly a reinterpretation rather than a fundamentally new method.

The theoretical contribution is weaker than claimed. Proposition 1 relies on a continuous-time, vanishing-step-size limit and a fairly loose construction of annealed verifier functions. It does not rigorously establish that practical finite-step training-free guidance with recurrence behaves as Langevin MCMC, and the 'first to unify' claim is overstated given prior work on guidance, composition, and MCMC.

Evaluation is incomplete for a top-tier venue. The image-generation experiments compare mainly against Best-of-N, not against the closest search-based diffusion baselines or other inference-time scaling methods, making it hard to assess whether the gains are due to the proposed framework or simply any search strategy.

Compute comparisons are not fully convincing. The paper reports reduced compute in terms of verifier calls or particles in some plots, but does not consistently provide wall-clock compute, memory, or matched-budget comparisons across all domains. It is therefore unclear whether the method is practically more efficient than strong alternatives.

Offline RL results are only competitive, not uniformly better. The method matches QGPO/D-QL on average while requiring substantial task-specific hyperparameter tuning, which weakens the training-free advantage and raises reproducibility concerns.

Global search design is under-ablated. Critical choices such as thresholds, temperature schedules, evaluation timesteps, backtracking depth, and buffer behavior are not systematically analyzed; DFS performance appears highly sensitive to these parameters, yet sensitivity and failure cases are not reported.

The paper relies heavily on task-specific verifiers, including oracle Maze verifiers, pretrained Q-functions, and external VQA/detection models. This makes the central inference-scaling claims verifier-dependent and less general than presented, and the verifier-hacking issue is only partially addressed via 'double-verifier' without a deeper analysis.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. The abstract states significant gains in performance and efficiency across all tasks, but the RL results are mostly comparable to existing methods, and image evaluations are limited to selected tasks, labels, and baselines.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and important problem: inference-time scaling for diffusion models, and frames it through classical search (local Langevin MCMC plus global BFS/DFS). The framework is general and unifies several existing ideas.

The theoretical connection between recurrent training-free guidance and annealed Langevin MCMC is a useful contribution; it provides principled insight into why recurrence helps avoid OOD samples by balancing verifier optimization against KL regularization toward the base manifold.
The empirical study is broad, spanning long-horizon planning, offline RL, and image generation, and shows training-free improvements and compute-efficiency gains over best-of-N in several settings.

The local search with verifier gradients is shown to be effective for maze planning and offline RL, where naive sampling fails; using a pretrained Q-function as verifier achieves competitive D4RL scores without retraining.

The global search methods (BFS-Resampling, BFS-Pruning, DFS with backtracking) are simple, practical, and empirically improve efficiency; DFS's difficulty-aware compute allocation is an interesting and well-demonstrated behavior.
The paper is generally clear, with useful pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, and appendix details that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is incremental: the local search is essentially existing training-free guidance/recurrent guidance interpreted as Langevin MCMC, while BFS/DFS are standard search heuristics adapted to diffusion. The closest inference-time scaling methods are not compared against in the image experiments, making the empirical case less convincing.

Image-generation evaluation is weak in terms of baselines: comparisons are mainly to Best-of-N, not to Ma et al. 2025, SMC/Feynman-Kac steering, or other training-free/guided diffusion methods. ImageNet FID and accuracy are far from standard conditional generation results, despite the unconditional-model setting.

Offline RL gains are modest and not clearly state-of-the-art: average 86.1 vs. 86.6 for QGPO and 86.3 for D-QL; several individual tasks are substantially below the best baselines. Baseline numbers are largely taken from prior work rather than re-evaluated under a unified protocol, and per-task hyperparameter tuning raises fairness concerns.

Planning evaluation depends on a handcrafted ground-truth maze verifier and mostly compares against best-of-N; it does not include other diffusion-planning or search-based planning baselines. This makes it unclear how well the approach scales to imperfect, sparse, or learned verifiers.

The theoretical results are asymptotic and rely on continuous-time/small-step approximations; they do not provide finite-step guarantees for the practical algorithm, and the global search procedures lack convergence or optimality analysis.

The method's practical applicability is limited by verifier requirements: differentiable verifiers for local search and reliable verifiers for global search. Verifier hacking is acknowledged, but the double-verifier mitigation is only lightly evaluated and task-specific.
Reproducibility could be strengthened by a clear code/reproducibility statement and released implementation; the paper provides extensive details but no explicit artifact link in the manuscript.

strengths: Presents a unified framework that connects classical BFS/DFS with local Langevin MCMC for inference-time scaling of diffusion models.
Provides a useful theoretical unification between recurrent training-free guidance and annealed Langevin MCMC, including a convergence analysis.
The improved BFS design (Increase, Max, SSP) consistently outperforms prior particle/tree-search methods on SDv1.5 and SDXL across compute budgets.
DFS with threshold-based adaptive backtracking achieves improved compute-performance Pareto on CompBench and demonstrates instance-adaptive compute allocation.
Scaling local search via annealed Langevin MCMC improves long-horizon planning and offline RL, and joint local+global scaling is shown to outperform scaling either component alone.
The double-verifier strategy reduces reward hacking/OOD samples in conditional ImageNet generation and improves accuracy/FID over single-verifier guidance.
Extensive experiments span image generation, planning, offline RL, and policy distillation, with substantial implementation details and hyperparameter search.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the BFS design mostly unifies and ablates existing particle/tree-search components, DFS is a relatively simple threshold-backtracking scheme, and local search is essentially scaling recurrent TFG with a new theoretical interpretation.

The theoretical convergence bound assumes strong log-concavity/log-smoothness of the composed target distribution, which may not hold for practical diffusion-plus-verifier objectives; the practical algorithm therefore lacks rigorous guarantees in realistic settings.
Empirical gains in image generation are sometimes modest (e.g., small improvements over DAS/FK-steering), and the double-verifier evaluation uses only 256 samples with relatively high FID values.
Offline RL results are not state-of-the-art on average (86.1 vs QGPO 86.6 and D-QL 86.3), with several per-task results trailing training-based baselines substantially.
The double-verifier approach is heuristic and lacks deep theoretical justification; it also assumes access to multiple independent verifiers, which may not always be available.
Some claims such as 'first adaptive DFS' and 'first joint scaling' may be partially dependent on concurrent work and are only compared in the appendix.
Additional hyperparameters are introduced and acknowledged as a limitation, with automated tuning left for future work.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: inference-time scaling/control for diffusion models via search.
It provides a useful conceptual unification of several BFS/particle-based methods and ablates design choices (resampling, scoring, tempering), yielding a stronger practical BFS variant.
The DFS-style adaptive backtracking mechanism is simple and shows promising compute adaptivity in text-to-image generation.
The attempt to connect training-free guidance with recurrence to annealed Langevin MCMC is interesting and could be of theoretical interest if properly developed.
The empirical coverage is broad, spanning image generation, long-horizon planning, offline RL, and reward hacking, with some notable gains in decision-making tasks.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the proposed BFS is largely a recombination of existing components (SSP resampling from DAS, Max scoring from FK-steering, Increase tempering from DAS), and the ablation gains are modest. DFS-style threshold backtracking is intuitive but not clearly beyond prior tree/backtracking search methods.

The local-search method is essentially training-free guidance with more recurrence, implemented in the TFG hyperparameter space; the claimed theoretical unification is not fully convincing and relies on strong assumptions (e.g., strong log-concavity) that do not hold for typical compositional diffusion targets.

The theoretical result in Theorem 1 is only for the recurrence-with-guidance approximation, but the paper uses it to justify exact Langevin MCMC sampling; the connection to the actual algorithm and the asymptotic weight lambda is not rigorously established.

Evaluation issues: for BFS image generation, only FK-steering is stated to use official code, while other baselines may be reimplemented, making comparisons uncertain. The reported gains over DAS are small and within variance in several cases.

The double-verifier ImageNet experiment reports extremely poor FID (e.g., 118–171) and low class accuracy, yet it is presented as mitigating reward hacking; this is not a convincing demonstration of high-quality conditional generation.

Offline RL claims are overstated: the method is comparable to, not clearly better than, strong training-based baselines on average, and the paper occasionally refers to 'ground-truth Q-functions,' which would be unrealistic and confusing; learned Q-functions are what should be used.
The planning experiment lacks comparison with standard planning baselines and only compares local-search variants, making the significance of the gains less clear.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code link is explicitly given in the manuscript, and several implementation details (e.g., exact baseline tuning, compute accounting for training-based methods) are insufficiently specified.
The paper is dense and includes typos/inconsistencies (e.g., duplicate variables in the compositional generation equation, unclear notation around verifier/conditioning), affecting clarity.

strengths: The paper presents a principled and unified framework for inference-time scaling of diffusion models by connecting classical search (BFS/DFS/backtracking) with local Langevin MCMC search. The conceptual framing is clear and well motivated.

The BFS design-space analysis is useful: it unifies prior particle/SMC and tree-search methods such as SVDD, DAS, and FK-steering, and derives an improved BFS variant with stronger empirical performance.

The proposed DFS-style adaptive backtracking search is a novel and practical addition for diffusion inference-time scaling. It enables compute allocation to harder instances without requiring known difficulty labels and shows efficiency gains over BFS/BoN.

The local search component via annealed Langevin MCMC is theoretically grounded. Proposition 1 connects recurrent training-free guidance to annealed Langevin MCMC, and Theorem 1 provides a convergence-style bound, giving useful insight into why recurrence mitigates OOD/adversarial samples.

The joint scaling of local and global search is a meaningful contribution. The paper demonstrates that neither alone is sufficient in challenging decision-making domains, and the resulting Pareto frontier is supported across planning, offline RL, and image generation tasks.

The empirical evaluation is broad and includes diverse domains: text-to-image compositional generation, long-horizon PointMaze planning, D4RL offline RL, distillation, and ImageNet conditional generation. The appendix provides extensive implementation details and hyperparameters.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: the authors use official codebases for baselines, report hyperparameter searches, compute budgets in NFEs, and include detailed experimental setups in the appendix.
The paper is well written and clearly structured, with helpful diagrams and pseudocode for BFS, DFS, and resampling.
weaknesses: The BFS contribution is largely a systematic recombination and ablation of existing design choices (tempering, scoring, resampling) rather than a fundamentally new search algorithm. The improved BFS is useful, but its novelty is somewhat incremental.

Some claims of being the "first" are potentially fragile given concurrent work such as ABCD and EvoSearch. The paper discusses concurrent methods, but the exact novelty boundary for adaptive DFS and joint local/global scaling could be sharper.

The theoretical convergence theorem relies on assumptions such as bounded support, strong log-concavity, and log-smoothness that are unlikely to hold for complex diffusion model distributions and composed verifier objectives. The bound is therefore more illustrative than directly applicable to the realistic setting.

The role of non-differentiable verifiers is not fully addressed. While global search can use black-box or VLM verifiers, the local Langevin MCMC search depends on gradient access to the verifier, limiting applicability in some realistic tasks.

Offline RL results are not uniformly superior to training-based baselines. TTS is comparable to QGPO/D-QL on average (86.1 vs. 86.6/86.3) and relies on per-environment hyperparameter tuning, with some large variance (e.g., Walker2d Medium-Replay ±9.7). This weakens the strength of the central claim in that domain.

The image-generation evaluations are relatively limited: text-to-image comparisons mostly use N=4/8 and a single reward model, and the double-verifier experiment reports only 256 ImageNet samples with still-high FID. Larger-scale and more comprehensive image evaluations would strengthen the claims.

The framework introduces several hyperparameters (thresholds, tempering, scoring, guidance strengths, backtracking depth), and the paper acknowledges this only briefly. Practical deployment may require substantial tuning, and sensitivity analysis is partial.
Compute comparisons are based on NFEs, which is useful, but wall-clock efficiency and implementation-level overheads are not fully reported. This makes practical efficiency claims harder to assess.

The reward-hacking mitigation via double verifiers is interesting but preliminary. It is not analyzed theoretically, and the experimental validation is limited to a small conditional ImageNet setting.
